chapter_title: Open File Formats and Version Control
learning_objective: The learner will judge whether each of ten files is a good source, an acceptable source, or a poor source for revising a resource, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** file-format-triage
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate
**Bloom Verb:** judge
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge whether each of ten files is a good source, an acceptable source, or a poor source for revising a resource, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Source Format, Open File Format, Markdown, HTML, Word Processing File, PDF-Only Distribution (all defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each file the learner commits one of three bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the format table is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) A PDF is a good source because it is an open standard. (2) A picture of text can be edited. (3) A word processing file is always a poor source. **Instructional Rationale:** Judging a file against criteria is an Evaluate-level action. Ten files that mix open and closed formats, text and pictures, and editable and locked files make the learner apply the same criteria each time: can the structure be changed with free tools? **Content:** The three bins: Good source (open format that keeps structure and opens in free tools), Acceptable source (editable, but depends on particular software or loses some structure), and Poor source (cannot be edited as structured content with free tools). The ten files: | # | File shown to the learner | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | lesson.md, a Markdown text file | Good source | Plain text in an open format that any editor opens. | | 2 | lesson.odt, an OpenDocument text file | Good source | An international open standard that free software opens. | | 3 | lesson.docx, a Word document | Acceptable source | Editable in many programs, though full fidelity depends on particular software. | | 4 | slides.pptx, a slide file | Acceptable source | Editable, but it depends on particular software to display exactly. | | 5 | diagram.svg, a vector drawing | Good source | An open web standard, and shapes and text stay editable. | | 6 | diagram.png, a picture with no original drawing file | Poor source | A flat picture of a diagram, so its shapes and words cannot be edited. | | 7 | data.csv, a table saved as plain text | Good source | Plain text that any spreadsheet or editor opens. | | 8 | sim.html with sim.js, a simulation's web code | Good source | Readable, editable web code in open formats. | | 9 | lesson.pdf, offered with no other file | Poor source | A PDF records how pages look, not how the content is built. | | 10 | scan.jpg, a photo of a printed page | Poor source | It is a picture of text and not text, so no structure exists to edit. | **Provenance:** The files are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The format judgments follow the chapter sections "Open File Format" and "Common Source Formats". **Rules:** Each file has exactly one correct bin. Five files are Good, two are Acceptable, and three are Poor. A file offered alongside editable sources would be judged differently, and the sim states that these files are offered without other sources. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one file at a time, with the three bin definitions. 2. The learner places the file in a bin, and the placement is committed. 3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text. 4. After file 10 the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 10 files in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 10 correct on the first attempt". At 8 or more it adds "You can judge a source." Below 8 it lists the Why text of each missed file. **Starting State:** The first file, the three bin definitions, and three empty bins. The question shown is "Is this file a good source for revising the resource?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's format table lists Markdown, HTML, OpenDocument, Word, CSV, SVG, and PDF, and says a PDF alone is a poor source.
